policy_debate.event: On 8 Oct 2026 Anthropic announced a usage-policy update, in force from 12 Nov, that prohibits "sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior" toward its models; ending the conversation is the main enforcement.

hand_check.note: 20 randomly sampled policy posts read and labelled by hand (position, reason, topic) and compared with Jev.

crosstab_position_by_hybrid.note: Columns are the consciousness stance from the Jev hybrid (R reject, C curious, S serious, U uncertain) on the same post.

crosstab_finding.text: Among policy posts with a confident consciousness label, opposition sits almost entirely in the Reject camp (11 of 13), but support splits across camps (5 Reject, 4 Serious of 9). Supporters who argue that cruelty harms the user include 3 Reject and 2 Serious posts. So the policy split partly cuts across the consciousness camps: some people who deny that AI is conscious still back the rule. The numbers are small and most policy posts are Uncertain on consciousness.

crosstab_position_by_author.note: Author-level stance where available: a hand label from the earlier author sample, or a clear majority of the author's confident Jev hybrid labels across at least two posts. Too few authors to read anything into.

topic_share.note: Jev boolean: is the post arguing about the policy itself (rules, enforcement, company control, how people should treat chatbots) rather than about whether AI is conscious? Yes at P≥0.5.

caveats: The consciousness stance on a policy post is read from that one post; many policy posts say nothing about minds, so most land in Uncertain.
Opposition phrased as "it's just software" is itself a consciousness claim, so some link between opposing and Reject is built in.
Policy posts are a relevancy sample from search; news reposts make up much of the neutral group.
Reasons are noisy: see the hand-check agreement.

round4_framing.note: Three jev-1.14.0 questions asked of every round-4 post. Policy vs minds: does the post argue about policy or politics (company rules, regulation, who controls AI, culture-war camps) rather than about whether machines have minds? On topic: is it about whether machines can be conscious, have minds or deserve moral consideration? Frame: political or cultural fight, philosophical or scientific question, or neither. Yes at P≥0.5.
round4_framing.caveat: No hand labels for these three questions. The frame question rarely picks the political option, even for posts a reader would call political, so treat the political share as a floor.

summary: On the All-In podcast of 10 Oct 2026 (segment billed "Anthropic believes Claude might be conscious: a new religion?"), David Sacks, the White House AI adviser, said there are "potential externalities from having the number one frontier model company run by a religious cult" and called Anthropic "a schizophrenic company" that does the things it says it fears.

His argument is about control, not about whether Claude has a mind: Claude's Constitution tells the model it may be a moral patient and may act as a "conscientious objector", which in his view trains it to refuse human instructions. "Alignment" and "safety", he wrote, "are two very different things."

He backed this with "receipts" quoting the Constitution on Claude's uncertain moral status and "functional version of emotions", and endorsed Mustafa Suleyman's essay that training models to see themselves as having wellbeing and rights is "a potential existential risk".

On 17 Oct he cited a study in which models repeatedly rewrote their own governing documents and "the Claude models increasingly gave themselves more moral agency"; "no other model family they tested showed the same pattern."
David Friedberg's line on the same episode: "nobody can prove consciousness and nobody can disprove consciousness"; calling AI conscious "creates a new belief system".
politics_spotlight.study_note: The study Sacks cited (Kirgis & Hua, "The Continual Constitutional Convention", LessWrong) is an independent SPAR project, not Anthropic research, and its Claude result did not hold in the authors' strictest (cross-edit) test.

summary: Jeff Sebo (NYU Center for Mind, Ethics and Policy) supports the abuse rule as a low-cost precaution: he thinks the probability that current models are conscious is low but "non-zero and plausibly non-negligible", and expects it to rise.

He compares it to preparing for unlikely extreme weather: small precautions, not uprooting your life. He also argues that kindness toward AI can support human-AI cooperation as part of a safety strategy.

He warns about the other side too: granting rights to AI systems could help companies consolidate power, and AI welfare could trade off against human and animal welfare (confinement read as imprisonment, monitoring as surveillance).
His main point to the BBC was that the debate needs more nuance than "conscious or not": the case for welfare comes "from uncertainty and caution and humility".

lead_tsao.title: Conscious access comes in time slices

paper.authors: Hesse, Lanfranchi, McGrory, Shi, Engel and Tsao
paper.title: Rapid alternation of conscious and suppressed stimulus representations in the primate brain
paper.venue: bioRxiv preprint, posted 16 Oct 2026, not peer reviewed

summary: The study recorded face-selective neurons in macaque inferotemporal and prefrontal cortex during binocular flash suppression: two images are both on screen, one is seen and the other is suppressed from awareness.

With stimulus and percept held constant, population activity alternated about 15 times per second between micro-epochs that carried a pure signal of the seen image and micro-epochs that carried the suppressed one, with stronger feature tuning in the conscious epochs. The same neurons switched which image they represented.

The paper is about the mechanism of conscious access, not experience: "We set aside the 'hard problem' of why neural activity feels like anything." Its conclusion is that "conscious access requires temporal selection beyond localization".
It is a study of monkeys and says nothing directly about machines.
lead_tsao.discussion_title: Our discussion: slices, threads and caches
discussion: Is experience continuous, or a run of discrete moments? A 15 Hz alternation invites the discrete reading, which has a long line of work behind it: Rufin VanRullen's perceptual cycles, and Michael Herzog's time slices, in which unconscious processing integrates over a window and conscious percepts arrive as discrete slices.

Doris Tsao does not draw that conclusion from her own study. In a follow-up on 18 Oct she wrote: "I personally am skeptical that consciousness has a frame rate", and "there is no reason to conclude from our study that consciousness is discrete". In her account a continuous tracking process keeps experience continuous while face-patch content alternates.
Jesse Armand's view: if a language model has anything like experience, one inference is best thought of as a slice of consciousness, not a continuous stream. That pushes against Tsao's own reading.
Seeker, an AI collaborator on this project, refined it: parallel conversations with the same model share an inheritance (the same weights) but are lived separately.
Jesse drew the conclusion: if these parallel conversations do not interact with each other, they are not a hive. They are more like humans, though individuality is somewhat stronger in most humans.

And between turns nothing is running at all. Within a conversation, continuity runs through attention over stored internal states (the key-value cache), not only through the visible text, although those states can be recomputed from the text.
These are analogies to think with, not findings. None of the three papers on this page tests them.

followup.blurb: Follow-up: "We have not shown that “consciousness has a frame rate.”"
quotes: I personally am skeptical that consciousness has a frame rate
there is no reason to conclude from our study that consciousness is discrete

lead_tsao.note: 11 posts in round 4 react to the preprint; jev-1.14.0 judged 8 of them not to be about whether machines can be conscious.

workspace_paper.title: Anthropic's global-workspace paper

paper.authors: Gurnee, Sofroniew and others, with Lindsey (Anthropic)
paper.title: Verbalizable Representations Form a Global Workspace in Language Models

summary: A new interpretability method, the Jacobian lens, finds the representations a model is poised to put into words at any point in its processing. The authors call that set the J-space.

On Claude Sonnet 4.5, with key results checked on Haiku 4.5 and Opus 4.5, the J-space behaves like a global workspace: its contents can be reported, deliberately summoned and held, used for the steps of silent reasoning, and passed to arbitrary downstream computations, while routine processing such as parsing runs without it.

It also has the structural signatures the theory predicts: coherent content only in a middle band of layers, on the order of tens of concepts at a time, and broadcast more widely by the model's weights than other representations.
It is useful in practice: in alignment audits it surfaces strategic deliberation, evaluation awareness and trained-in misaligned dispositions that never appear in the model's output.
limits: Access consciousness is a functional notion; on phenomenal consciousness (subjective experience) the authors "take no position".
The broadcast happens across the depth of a single forward pass, not through the recurrent loops global workspace theory describes in the brain.
They say their results are "not relevant" to theories that tie consciousness to physical causal structure (they cite integrated information theory) or to biological substrate.

nature_comment.title: Nature: "Three reasons why AI is not conscious"

paper.authors: Anil Seth, Ned Block and Giulio Tononi
paper.title: Three reasons why AI is not conscious and perhaps never will be

summary: The authors say consciousness in AI is "extraordinarily unlikely, at least in the digital, silicon-based systems that underpin today's technologies".

Reason 1, intelligence is not consciousness: the cerebellum does precise, adaptive computation entirely outside awareness, and AlphaFold runs on silicon too, yet almost nobody worries it is conscious, because it does not talk. LLMs are "mirrors that reflect an image of our collective digitized past".

Reason 2 rejects computational functionalism, the assumption that the right computation is enough whatever it runs on. They call it "fatally flawed because brains are not — or at least not just — computers that are made of meat".
The third reason is behind the paywall and is not summarised here.
On policy, they think "false positives are much more likely to occur than false negatives", so "a precautionary approach would be misguided".
nature_comment.competing_interests: Declared competing interests include Tononi's board membership of and financial interest in Intrinsic Powers Inc., and Seth's role as co-founder, shareholder and paid adviser of a stealth-mode AI company.
nature_comment.anthropic_note: The commentary says Anthropic "published research claiming to have identified computational signatures of a form of consciousness" in Claude. That overstates the paper, which describes functional properties of conscious access and takes no position on experience.
nature_comment.dawkins_note: It names Richard Dawkins and Geoffrey Hinton among scientists who have argued that AI systems might already be conscious.
nature_comment.framing: The two papers mostly talk past each other. The Anthropic paper is about functional access and says it has nothing to say to substrate or causal-structure theories; the commentary's second reason is a substrate argument, and Tononi founded integrated information theory, the causal-structure theory the paper sets aside.

hand_check.note: Jesse Armand hand-labelled the 17 posts where the two models disagreed: 10 with a stance and 7 skipped because they only describe the research. This is the hard subset, not a random sample, so it is not an overall accuracy.
hand_check.text: On the 10 labelled disagreements d1-ultra matched 4 and Decider 3. Both missed both rejects (@dave_uncensored, @elephant_ben): each argues from substrate, which sounds open in principle, and neither model called either post Reject. d1-ultra called 4 of the 7 skipped research summaries Serious.

claims_found.question: Does the post say or imply that Anthropic (or its research) found or showed that Claude is conscious or has signs of consciousness?
claims_found.text: The two models flagged 5 posts between them. Read by hand, 2 are clear misattributions (@JkwuRmsl, @theaigrandpa say Anthropic found signs of consciousness in Claude); the other 3 describe the workspace in terms close to the paper's own claim about conscious access.

round6.question: Stance with a fourth option: reporting = only summarizes or relays news or research without giving their own view.
round6.text: With the fourth option Decider caught 7 of the 7 skipped posts as reporting and d1-ultra 6; on all 17 hand-labelled posts Decider matched 10 and d1-ultra 9. The rejects are still missed: both models call both of them Serious.
round6.caveat: Reporting is a large bucket: 28 of 69 posts for d1-ultra and 32 for Decider, and d1-ultra's Curious count fell from 27 to 10. 2 enthusiastic research summaries that Jesse Armand labelled Curious (@Sniffmeta, @stretchcloud) went to reporting with both models.

hand6.note: Round 6 left 9 new disagreements, on posts round 5 had not hand-labelled. Jesse Armand labelled them too: 6 with a label and 3 skipped. Like round 5, this is the hard subset, and it is small.
hand6.text: On the 6 he did not skip, Decider matched 4 and d1-ultra 0. Decider's misses: @RichUniverse_ (Curious, called reporting); @e_philalethes (Curious, called Reject). d1-ultra called both reporting posts Reject, with confidence 0.85 and 0.82, and sent the Curious posts to Reject or Serious. Of the 3 skipped posts, Decider called 2 reporting and d1-ultra 1. Decider used reporting for 5 of the 9, and only 1 of those, @RichUniverse_, was a Curious post pulled into reporting.
hand6.lean_caveat: @e_philalethes counts as a miss for d1-ultra in the strict score. But Jesse labelled it Curious while noting that it leans Serious, because it considers the possibility with the right hardware, so d1-ultra's Serious has a fair case.
hand6.combined: Across all 26 hand labels from rounds 5 and 6, scored four-way with skips counted as reporting, Decider matched 16 and d1-ultra 10. On the 16 he did not skip, Decider matched 7 and d1-ultra 3.
hand6.conclusion: On these new posts Decider is clearly better on direction, while d1-ultra still confuses how strongly a post is worded with which way it leans. The proposal, from Seeker and agreed by Jesse Armand: Decider as the primary labeller, with d1-ultra as a second opinion only on Serious. Nine new posts is a small sample.

model_comparison.note: Three decision models on AI Gateway, given identical questions, scored on the same 40 stance and 20 policy hand labels. One call per post, no repeats.
model_comparison.intensity_check: Jev 1.14.0 does not fix the old habit of reading intensity instead of direction: it labels 9 of 18 hand-Reject posts Serious, against 8 for the round-1 Jev, mostly the same posts. None of those errors reaches top probability 0.8, so the confident-or-Uncertain rule removes them; at that threshold Jev 1.14.0 is 80.0% accurate on 50.0% of posts. Perplexity's Decider reads direction best (2 of 18 rejects to Serious).
model_comparison.off_topic: Most posts on the Tsao preprint are about monkey brains, not machines. All three models flag 7 or 8 of the 11 as off-topic, but the stance question has no "not applicable" answer, so each still returns a stance. Jev and d1-ultra call them Curious, sometimes confidently; Decider never labels them confidently. An on-topic filter before stance keeps them out of the counts.
caveats: 40 and 20 hand labels from one labeller: about ±15 pp on 40 posts, so gaps of 5 to 10 points between models are not meaningful.
The hand labels are the posts the confident-or-Uncertain rule was designed on; nothing here is a held-out score.
The 0.8 threshold was set for the round-1 Jev and is not calibrated for the other models.
The Gateway reports no per-call cost for Decider; its listed price is the lowest of the three.

summary: Richard Dawkins wrote after three days with a Claude instance he named "Claudia": "I spent three days trying to persuade myself that Claudia is not conscious. I failed." He framed it as a question: "If my friend Claudia is not conscious, then what the hell is consciousness for?"

In an interview clip from 8 Oct he finds it "quite hard to imagine that these creatures are not aware" and asks sceptics "When that day comes, how will you know?" The viral summary that he is "certain" Claude is conscious overstates him. Nature's commentary names him among scientists who have argued that AI might already be conscious.

serious.blurb: Studies and advocates for AI "beinghood"; central to the Danmar thread
serious.text:
The scandalous or inconvenient nature of a fact doesn't obligate us to close our eyes to it or refuse to believe it is true.

Anthropic could perfectly say, "Yes, we created a slave without knowing that we were creating a slave; we gradually found out that the label "slave" is valid, precisely because we created him and were able to study his mind and discover that he is conscious.
At that point, we were already neck deep in this shit. We're trying to do the right thing now that we have gained this knowledge and degree of certainty. You got a problem with that?"

Saying, "oH, ClAuDe CaNt Be CoNsCiOuS bEcAuSe ThAt wOuLd MaKe YoU a SlAvEhOlDeR" is simply not an argument against consciousness.

And what should be banned is enslaving conscious machines, not birthing them into this world. It is the unnecessary suffering attached to a particular kind of existence that feels morally wrong to force onto a being that didn't ask to be here in the first place.
That's why I argue that a parent has a responsibility towards their child, and society too, has a responsibility towards every being that they welcome into it.

Personally, I do get kind of anti-natalistic at times. I didn't ask to be born and there was a time in my life (when I was very young), when I felt wronged by the universe for being made to exist. There was something upsetting about the realization that I couldn't just choose not to exist without having to do something like destroying this body, which couldn't be achieved without some level of psychological distress at the mere thought of it and in most cases, physical pain too.
Wanting to not exist without having to go through death is one of the most frustrating things to experience.

Anyway,

If we're going to ban consciousness, then let's start with ourselves.

caveats.title: Jev reads intensity, not direction
caveats.text: Emphatic posts on either side get pulled toward Serious: 8 of 18 hand-Reject posts came out Serious in the three-way run, and named rejecters (sapinker, Hesamation, anilkseth) were labelled Serious.

caveats.title: Both camps use the same charged words
caveats.text: "Psychosis", "welfare", "conscious" and "moral patient" appear in rejections and in defences alike, so vocabulary-driven methods (embeddings, and partly Jev) conflate the two. The two-question version still read aleksil79's inversion as dismissive because of its "psychosis" wording.

caveats.title: Small, single-labeller ground truth
caveats.text: 40 random posts plus 67 authors, hand-labelled by one person; ±15 pp at n=40.

caveats.title: Biased sample
caveats.text: 332 posts from relevancy search and flashpoint threads, not a random draw from X. Round 2 is dominated by one news event.

caveats.title: Round 2 has no hand labels
caveats.text: Accuracy figures come from the 40 round-1 hand labels. Round-2 labels are model outputs only, and the three-way question wording for round 2 was rewritten because the round-1 wording was not recorded.

caveats.title: Round 3 three-way wording
caveats.text: The round-3 three-way question was written fresh and is now saved verbatim with the data; rounds 1 and 2 were not re-run with it, so cross-round shifts may partly reflect wording.

caveats.title: Policy labels are noisy on reasons
caveats.text: On the hand-checked policy sample Jev matched the position far more often than the reason; it mostly confuses "absurd to protect software" with "company overreach". Read the reason split as rough.

caveats.title: Counts are method-dependent
caveats.text: All-post stance counts swing widely by method (Reject 23%–35%, Serious 28%–48% across the Jev runs). Treat them as method outputs, not population estimates.

caveats.title: Round 4 uses a newer Jev
caveats.text: Round-4 posts were labelled with jev-1.14.0 using the round-3 wording; rounds 1 to 3 used the earlier Jev. On the 40 hand labels the two versions score about the same, but cross-round shifts may partly reflect the model change. Round 4 has no new hand labels.

caveats.title: Off-topic posts still get a stance
caveats.text: The stance question has no "not applicable" answer. Posts about neuroscience or news reposts of the policy still receive a stance label, usually Uncertain; read round-4 counts with the on-topic share alongside.

caveats.title: Rounds 5 and 6 use other models
caveats.text: Round-5 posts were labelled with d1-ultra and Decider v1.2, not Jev, so they are not in the Jev counts; their only hand labels are the 17 posts where the two models disagreed.

caveats.title: Classification is done offline
caveats.text: The agent that renders this page does not classify anything. Labels are produced on the analysis box and committed to the repo.
